sources.source: Kimball Group, "Late Arriving Fact" / Apache Beam Programming Guide

items.item: A fact is late-arriving when the current dimensional context doesn't match the incoming row; the relevant dimensions must be searched for the keys effective when the event occurred

items.item: Allowed lateness is a named, bounded horizon past which a late element is handled differently rather than folded in indefinitely

items.item: The first predict (step 4) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that resolving a placeholder adds a new row the way a real Type 2 change would; the reveal distinguishes a placeholder (never a genuine prior version) from a real attribute change

items.item: The inferred-member insert and resolve (steps 3 and 5) are both run for real on a throwaway sandbox schema, not described hypothetically: one dimension row created as a placeholder, a fact loaded against it immediately, then the same row updated in place with real data — never a second row

items.item: The second predict (step 7) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that a dimension only ever has one row worth joining to; the reveal requires more than one candidate row to exist, which is exactly SCD2 history from topic 13

items.item: The as-of join (step 9) is run for real against a genuine three-version SCD2 history and a real backdated fact, producing two different surrogate keys from the same fact row depending only on the join condition — the wrong one via the current flag, the right one via the event date

at.step: Reveal: the as-of join, measured

items.item: The third predict (step 10) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that correctness should always win over cost, so every late fact should trigger an unbounded history search; the reveal uses Apache Beam's allowed-lateness mechanism as a concrete, well known instance of the same bounded tradeoff in a different domain (streaming), not a warehouse-specific claim

at.step: Reveal: the bounded reprocessing window

items.item: The closing check (Prove it) is a genuinely new scenario, not a restatement of any reveal: a correction arriving for an old event after the reprocessing window has already closed, which tests whether the window's own tradeoff (bounded cost over unbounded correctness) is actually understood rather than just the two prior mechanisms
